blocks.md: One worker, many waiting jobs, no preemption. Short jobs improve average flow time, but a scheduler that always favors them can leave a long job waiting forever. Balance **latency** with **eventual service**.

blocks.label: FIG 1
blocks.caption: Once A starts it owns the worker until tick 6. Better ordering happens only at idle boundaries.

blocks.title: Flow time includes waiting
blocks.md: `flow = completion - arrival`. Running a short job first often lowers the mean, while aging or a maximum-wait rule prevents long jobs from starving.

blocks.output: one valid policy: B → C → A
blocks.explain: Shortest-work-first gives B and C fast completion, but the policy still records A's wait. As A ages, its priority must eventually outrank newly arriving short jobs.

items: Never run a job before arrival or while another job owns the worker.
Mark a returned job running immediately because same-tick callbacks may follow.
The harness can present several same-tick arrivals before the idle progress callback.
Every waiting job must eventually run; deliberate idling with queued work fails.

items.title: Start with FIFO
items.md: It establishes correct callback handling and guarantees progress.

items.title: Prefer short work
items.md: Use exact `EstimatedWork` to reduce mean flow time when the worker becomes idle.

items.title: Add aging
items.md: Increase priority with wait time or enforce a maximum wait so tail latency remains bounded.

blocks.title: Read the metrics together
blocks.md: Mean flow rewards short-job ordering; p95 flow and starvation penalty expose policies that sacrifice old jobs. Peak state and scheduler work show the bookkeeping cost.
